content: The study by Shastri SS et al. evaluated the effectiveness of visual inspection, cytological testing, and HPV testing as screening methods for early detection of cervical neoplasia in Mumbai, India. This research, published in the Bulletin of the World Health Organization in 2005, highlighted the potential of these methods in resource-limited settings. Sodhani P et al. conducted a feasibility study to assess the characteristics of various cervical cancer screening modalities. Their findings, published in Cytopathology in 2006, aimed to develop alternative strategies for resource-constrained environments. Denny L et al. explored the relationship between human papillomavirus (HPV) infection and cervical disease in women infected with HIV-1. Their study, published in Obstetrics & Gynecology in 2008, provided insights into the unique challenges faced by this population. De Vuyst H et al. examined the prevalence and determinants of HPV infection and cervical lesions in HIV-positive women in Kenya. Their findings, published in the British Journal of Cancer in 2012, emphasized the importance of targeted screening in high-risk groups. Joshi S et al. investigated cervical neoplasia screening in HIV-infected women in India. Their study, published in AIDS in 2013, highlighted the need for tailored screening approaches in this vulnerable population. The Osmanabad District Cervical Screening Study Group conducted a cluster-randomized controlled trial comparing visual inspection, cytology, and HPV testing for cervical cancer screening in rural India. Their findings, published in the International Journal of Cancer in 2005, underscored the feasibility of implementing these methods in low-resource settings. Zhang HY et al. conducted a pilot study on HPV prevalence and cervical intraepithelial neoplasia among HIV-infected women in Yunnan Province, China. Their research, published in the Asian Pacific Journal of Cancer Prevention in 2012, provided valuable data on the burden of cervical disease in this population. The expert panel recommended a screening strategy involving HPV testing followed by visual inspection with acetic acid (VIA) and treatment with cryotherapy (or LEEP if cryotherapy is not suitable). This approach was preferred over cytology-based screening followed by colposcopy and treatment, as it may require fewer resources and fewer follow-up visits. The recommendation applies to women regardless of HIV status, although the evidence supporting this strategy is of low quality. The panel noted that while the benefits of both strategies are similar, cytology-based programs may demand more resources due to the need for quality control, provider training, and longer waiting times. Additionally, colposcopy requires a second visit, which could lead to higher rates of loss to follow-up. The evidence for the diagnostic accuracy of HPV testing followed by VIA compared to cytology followed by colposcopy is limited and of low quality. The benefits and harms of these strategies are likely similar, but HPV testing followed by VIA may detect slightly fewer cancers. Resource implications favor HPV testing followed by VIA, as cytology programs require additional training, quality control, and waiting time, and colposcopy necessitates a second visit. The panel emphasized the importance of a screen-and-treat approach over no screening, as qualitative studies have shown that women find screening tests and immediate treatment acceptable once they decide to participate. High value was placed on the resources required for implementation, with fewer resources potentially needed for HPV testing followed by VIA compared to cytology-based programs.
